assessment.1. Interference with freedom of expressi: There was a clear interference with the applicant’s Article 10 rights. He was prosecuted for a tweet, convicted of defamation, fined, exposed to an alternative sentence of imprisonment, ordered to delete the post, and required to pay compensation; the statement was also formally declared unfounded (see paragraphs 8-12). Such measures plainly had a punitive and chilling effect.

assessment.2. Lawfulness and legitimate aim: The interference appears to have been prescribed by law, namely Articles 267, 269 and 271 of the Penal Code and section 26 of the Liability and Compensation Act (see paragraphs 13-18). The legal basis was accessible and sufficiently foreseeable for a social-media user. It also pursued a legitimate aim, namely the protection of the reputation and rights of another person, R.P. The decisive issue is therefore whether the interference was necessary in a democratic society.

assessment.3. Context of the speech and margin of a: The speech concerned a political figure and a matter of public interest. R.P. was the founder and leader of a right-wing anti-Islam party, had attracted major public attention through anti-Islam demonstrations and Koran burnings, and had been widely discussed in the media, including debate on whether he should be considered fascist or Nazi (see paragraphs 6-7). Even though he was not sitting in Parliament at the material time, he remained a prominent political actor who had deliberately entered public controversy. Under the Court’s case-law, expression in political debate and on matters of public concern enjoys strong protection and the margin of appreciation is narrow (see nos. 39954/08 and 40660/08).

assessment.4. Nature of the statement and factual b: The High Court itself treated the impugned remark as a value judgment rather than a statement of fact (see paragraph 11). Under the Court’s case-law, value judgments are not susceptible of proof, though they must have a sufficient factual basis (see no. 26958/95). Here, the applicant relied on R.P.’s public conduct and reputation: his ethnonationalist political profile, anti-Islam actions, Koran burnings, repeated extremist public interventions, prior convictions for racist speech, and the pre-existing public and media debate as to whether he was a fascist or Nazi (see paragraphs 6-7, 10-11). In that context, calling R.P. a 'Nazi' appears to be harsh political invective or rhetorical exaggeration, but not a wholly baseless attack.

assessment.5. Sufficiency of the domestic courts’ r: The domestic courts gave some Convention-based reasoning, but their reasons were likely not relevant and sufficient. First, they downplayed the public-interest context by saying that the tweet was merely a reply in a thread about the arrest of another person for calling a police officer an idiot (see paragraphs 5 and 11). Yet the applicant’s post was plainly about unequal tolerance of offensive speech and about the public role of R.P., which is itself a matter of public concern. Second, the High Court seems to have required a very high level of substantiation for a value judgment drawn from notorious public facts and debate (see paragraph 11), whereas Strasbourg case-law accepts a broader factual basis for polemical political expression, especially against public figures (see no. 26958/95).

assessment.6. Proportionality of the sanctions: The sanctions were substantial: ten day-fines totalling DKK 10,000, an alternative prison sentence of ten days, DKK 30,000 in compensation, a deletion order, and a declaration that the statement was unfounded (see paragraphs 9 and 11). Moreover, Danish law had recently tripled the normal level of fines and compensation for defamation (see paragraphs 15 and 18), which increases the chilling effect. In a case concerning political expression by a private individual on a public platform, these cumulative sanctions were likely disproportionate to the aim of protecting reputation.

assessment.7. Overall forecast: Given the political and public-interest context, R.P.’s status as a highly provocative public figure, the classification of the impugned remark as a value judgment, the existence of a sufficient factual basis in his public conduct, and the severity of the cumulative sanctions, the Court would likely find that Denmark failed to strike a fair balance under Article 10. The interference was therefore probably not necessary in a democratic society (see nos. 26958/95, 39954/08 and 40660/08).
